title: Phrasal Verbs
summary: Separable and inseparable patterns, three-part combinations, idiomatic meaning, and when a single formal verb reads better.

sections.heading: Phrasal Verb or Verb Plus Preposition
sections.body:
A **phrasal verb** is a verb plus a particle such as `up`, `off`, `out`, `down` or `on`, and the combined meaning is often unpredictable from the parts: `put off` means postpone, not place away. A verb with a **dependent preposition** is different: the verb keeps its ordinary meaning and simply requires that preposition, as in `depend on` or `refer to`.

The practical test is word order. A particle can move to the far side of a short object, so `turn the offer down` is possible, whereas a preposition is locked in front of its object and `depend the outcome on` is impossible.

Stress gives the same answer in speech. In `She looked UP the reference` the particle carries stress; in `She looked at the REFERENCE` the preposition does not.

examples.right: The organisers called off the match.
examples.note: `off` is a particle: the meaning is cancel, unrelated to direction.

examples.right: The organisers called the match off.
examples.note: The particle may follow the object, which a preposition never could.

examples.right: The outcome depends on the weather.
examples.wrong: The outcome depends the weather on.
examples.note: `on` here is a preposition and cannot move.

sections.heading: Separable and Inseparable
sections.body:
**Separable** phrasal verbs allow the object in either position: `turn down the offer` or `turn the offer down`. When the object is a pronoun the split becomes compulsory, so `turn it down` is the only possibility and `turn down it` is always wrong. This one rule accounts for a large share of phrasal-verb errors.

**Inseparable** phrasal verbs keep the particle beside the verb whatever follows: `look after the children` and `look after them`, `come across a problem` and `come across it`. Dictionaries mark this, and it is worth checking for any phrasal verb entering active use.

A long object stays on the far side even with a separable verb, since splitting would strand the particle far from its verb.

examples.right: The editor turned the proposal down.
examples.note: Separable: a short noun object may sit inside.

examples.right: The editor turned it down.
examples.note: A pronoun object must precede the particle.

examples.right: A technician will look after the equipment.
examples.wrong: A technician will look the equipment after.
examples.note: `look after` is inseparable.

examples.right: She turned down the generous offer from the consultancy.
examples.note: A long object stays after the particle even when the verb is separable.

sections.heading: Three-Part Phrasal Verbs
sections.body:
Some phrasal verbs carry a particle and a preposition together: `put up with`, `look forward to`, `come up with`, `get on with`, `cut down on`, `catch up on`, `run out of`, `keep up with`, `get rid of` and `face up to`.

These never separate. The object follows the whole group, and even a pronoun stays outside it: `put up with it`, never `put it up with`.

Because the final element is a preposition, a verb after it takes the `-ing` form: `look forward to hearing`, `get round to writing`, `face up to losing`.

examples.right: Few residents will put up with the noise for another year.
examples.wrong: Few residents will put the noise up with for another year.
examples.note: Three-part verbs never split, not even around a pronoun.

examples.right: We look forward to reading the final draft.
examples.wrong: We look forward to read the final draft.
examples.note: `to` is a preposition here, so the -ing form follows.

examples.right: The team came up with an inexpensive alternative.
examples.note: `come up with` means devise.

examples.right: Households have been asked to cut down on water use.
examples.note: `cut down on` means reduce.

sections.heading: Literal and Idiomatic Meaning
sections.body:
Many combinations have both a literal and an idiomatic reading, and only the context separates them. `The plane took off` describes movement; `Sales took off` does not. `She looked up at the ceiling` is direction; `She looked up the reference` is consultation.

Several phrasal verbs carry more than one idiomatic sense. `pick up` covers collecting a person, acquiring a skill informally and improving after a decline; `break down` covers failing mechanically, collapsing emotionally and analysing something into parts.

Storing them inside a short phrase rather than as a bare pair keeps the senses apart: `pick up a language`, `pick up a passenger`, `trade picked up`.

examples.right: The helicopter took off in poor visibility.
examples.note: Literal movement.

examples.right: Online enrolment took off once the fee was scrapped.
examples.note: Idiomatic: began to grow rapidly.

examples.right: He picked up conversational Portuguese in a single summer.
examples.note: `pick up` here means acquire informally.

examples.right: The article breaks the costs down by region.
examples.note: `break down` in its analytical sense, and separable in that use.

sections.heading: Register: Phrasal Verb or Single Verb
sections.body:
Phrasal verbs are ordinary English, not slang, and they belong in speech and in informal writing. In formal academic prose a single Latinate verb is often the better fit, and the mark comes from choosing deliberately rather than from avoiding phrasal verbs altogether.

The pairs worth knowing are `find out` and `discover`, `put off` and `postpone`, `bring about` and `cause`, `look into` and `investigate`, `carry out` and `conduct`, `point out` and `indicate`, `set up` and `establish`, `go up` and `increase`, `cut down on` and `reduce`, `deal with` and `address`, `get rid of` and `eliminate`, `come up with` and `devise`, `leave out` and `omit`.

The reverse error is also possible. A chain of Latinate verbs in the speaking tasks sounds stilted, and `find out` is the natural choice there.

examples.right: The agency carried out a survey of two thousand households.
examples.note: Neutral, and acceptable in most writing.

examples.right: The agency conducted a survey of two thousand households.
examples.note: The formal equivalent, better suited to a written report.

examples.right: The authors point out that the sample was small.
examples.note: In an essay, `indicate` or `note` lifts the register.

sections.heading: A Working Set for the Exam
sections.body:
A limited set, learned properly, is worth more than a long list read once. For academic content: `carry out`, `point out`, `bring about`, `look into`, `set up`, `break down`, `come up with`, `rule out`, `account for`, `focus on`, `take into account` and `result in`.

For everyday tasks and for describing an image: `go up`, `go down`, `level off`, `pick up`, `drop off`, `catch up`, `run out of`, `turn out`, `end up`, `take over`, `put up with` and `get on with`.

The second group repays the most preparation, because the graph description has to be produced under time pressure and `level off`, `go up` and `drop off` are the natural words for it.

examples.right: The figure rose sharply in 2019 and then levelled off.
examples.note: `level off` means stop rising or falling.

examples.right: The proposal turned out to be cheaper than expected.
examples.note: `turn out` means prove to be, and is inseparable in this sense.

examples.right: The committee ruled out any further increase.
examples.note: `rule out` means exclude; it separates around a pronoun, as in `ruled it out`.

slips: `turn down it` is always wrong. A pronoun object goes between verb and particle: `turn it down`.
Three-part verbs never split: `put up with it`, not `put it up with`.
`look forward to` ends in a preposition, so the -ing form follows: `look forward to meeting you`.
`look after` and `come across` are inseparable, so no object can sit inside them.
A phrasal verb is not slang, but in a written task the single verb usually reads better: `investigate` for `look into`, `postpone` for `put off`.
`bring about` means cause while `bring up` means raise a topic. The particle carries the meaning and cannot be guessed.

questions.prompt: The offer was clearly inadequate, so the board turned ___ without further discussion.
questions.explain: `turn down` is separable, and a pronoun object must sit between the verb and the particle. `turn down it` is never possible, however natural it looks beside `turn down the offer`.

questions.prompt: Residents said they could no longer ___ with the noise from the construction site.
questions.explain: `put up with` is a three-part verb meaning tolerate; all three elements stay together and the object follows them.

questions.prompt: The regulator is looking ___ the disappearance of several audit files.
questions.explain: `look into` means investigate. `look up` would mean consulting a reference and `look for` searching for something not yet lost from view.

questions.prompt: The reforms brought ___ a substantial fall in urban emissions within three years.
questions.explain: `bring about` means cause. `bring up` raises a topic and `bring out` publishes or reveals, so the particle alone decides the meaning.

questions.prompt: The government has promised to cut ___ on the use of single-use plastics.
questions.explain: `cut down on` is the three-part verb meaning reduce, and `cut back on` is an equally standard alternative; `cut off` and `cut out` would both change the sense entirely.

questions.prompt: The institute will ___ a series of field trials next spring.
questions.explain: `carry out` means perform or conduct, which is what happens to trials. `carry on` means continue and needs an activity already under way.

questions.prompt: He gets ___ well with the rest of the research team.
questions.explain: `get on with` is the British form and `get along with` the American one; both mean have a good relationship with, and both are correct.

questions.prompt: The organisers had to call ___ the outdoor sessions because of the storm.
questions.explain: `call off` means cancel. `call in` summons someone, `call up` telephones or conscripts, and neither works with an event.

questions.prompt: Engineers have come ___ with a cheaper method of desalinating seawater.
questions.explain: `come up with` means devise or produce an idea; without `up` the verb would mean encounter by chance.

questions.prompt: The committee looks forward to ___ the auditors' report next month.
questions.explain: The `to` of `look forward to` is the preposition of a three-part verb, not an infinitive marker, so an -ing form must follow.

questions.prompt: The seminar was ___ off until the following term because of the rail strike.
questions.explain: `put off` means postpone, and it is separable, so the passive keeps the particle after the participle.

questions.prompt: The report ___ out that emissions have fallen for three consecutive years.
questions.explain: `point out` means draw attention to a fact and is the only one of these that takes a that-clause; in formal writing `indicate` or `note` would raise the register.
